vignette:
Walter is a 73-year-old journalist who came to treatment decades into a career built on going toward catastrophe, yet he speaks about one assignment as if it never ended. He had been covering a man-made disaster when the scene turned suddenly chaotic and lethal. What has stayed with him most sharply is not a coherent narrative but fragments with the force of the present: press photographs from the aftermath, the metallic-bitter taste that got into his mouth and would not leave, the sickening fact that nothing about the situation had felt predictable from one second to the next. Even now he says the memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to him. At other times it is less disbelief than immediacy; the event replays like film, and when it comes back he feels as though he is there again rather than remembering from a distance.

In the months after, those fragments began attaching themselves to ordinary life. Related photos were especially potent. As a journalist he still works around image archives, newsroom layouts, and screens full of breaking stories, and when an editor drops disaster photos into a draft or he unexpectedly scrolls past an image resembling that assignment, he feels his body lock. He freezes when threatened, unable to move for a few moments, and after that he becomes rigid about where he sits, insisting on a chair with his back to the wall so he can scan the room. Unpredictable situations in the newsroom-sudden changes, unscheduled visitors, a raised voice from the corridor-bring the same shift in him. A particular taste can do it too, abruptly transporting him. When that happened, the trigger did not just startle him; it told him, with a force that felt undeniable, that he had become the kind of man who could be thrown out of himself by the smallest thing and would never again be fully in command of his own mind. In those moments the thought lands with him almost immediately that this is what his life has become-that he is a man who can be hijacked by anything at any time, and that he will never again be able to trust his own mind to stay in the present. On those days he is certain he will not be able to handle thinking about what happened, and the trigger itself seems to confirm his fear that his mind is no longer under his control.

Over time Walter has come to live as if danger announces itself in small signs that others miss. He listens at night for sounds that might mean someone is entering his home. Feeling this endangered so often became, for Walter, the most persuasive evidence that the disaster had changed him for good; if his body still acted as though catastrophe were imminent, he took that as proof that safety was no longer really available to him and that he himself was no longer normal. Living with that constant expectation of danger has gradually persuaded him that safety is no longer available to him in the ordinary way, and that the fact he has to monitor so relentlessly must mean the disaster left him permanently altered. In restaurants, interview settings, even his own office, he notices potential weapons first-letter openers, heavy lamps, the angle of a bottle on a table-and he cannot relax even when he knows, intellectually, that he is in a safe place. That state of watchfulness makes the world feel full of unpredictable situations, so his triggers multiply rather than narrow. A routine assignment can feel loaded because anything might change without warning, and his attention catches on photographs and sensory details before he is aware he is searching for them. When he is this keyed up, the old film starts running again. A creak in his apartment or the sight of an object that could be used as a weapon is enough to pull him back into the event, and afterward he takes it as further proof that something in him has been permanently altered. Each time the memory takes over so completely, he comes away convinced not just that the assignment was terrible, but that he himself has been changed into someone damaged and unlikely ever to feel normal again.

What frightens Walter most is not only the memory itself but what he has come to believe it means. He says that if he lets himself think about the disaster directly, he will not be able to handle it. Because he had come to believe he was too altered and too fragile to bear the memory, the way he managed his days began to feel like simple necessity: he kept himself distracted, spent impulsively for brief relief, and arranged his body near walls and exits because trusting himself to cope without those measures no longer seemed realistic to him. That conviction makes the fragments easier to stir up, not easier to contain; the more certain he is that remembering will overwhelm him, the more readily the old images and sensations break through, as if his mind keeps returning to the scene to test the danger he has assigned to it. He has come to believe he will never feel normal emotions again, and that nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore. Those convictions shape what he does every day. And the more he relied on those measures to get through the day, the more they seemed to prove their own premise to him: if he still needed to scan, position himself, and buy relief in quick bursts, then he must indeed be damaged, unable to cope, and unlikely to get his life back. He avoids letting his mind settle, buys things impulsively online and in stores for a brief sense of comfort or distraction, and arranges himself physically against walls and exits as if vigilance were the only thing holding him together. Over months, those habits have made reminders harder to escape: every restaurant without the right seat, every office chair with its back exposed, every image archive he tries to hurry past has become newly charged because his daily routines keep marking these situations as places where something is wrong. Yet the relief is short-lived. The spending leaves him ashamed and emptier; the constant positioning and scanning tell him the threat must be real; the effort not to think about the event only seems to make the memory more intrusive and unreal at the same time. He says it is like trying not to touch a bruise and ending up pressing on it all day.

The loop has tightened over the last year. Because he freezes when startled and spends so much energy monitoring his surroundings, he is less able to stay present during interviews and has pulled back from some assignments that once gave his life structure. At home he sits in restaurants only if he can face the door, and if he cannot, he leaves. In the office he dreads the image desk, yet when a photo catches him off guard the memory floods back so vividly that the rest of the day is organized around managing it. Each recurrence deepens his conviction that he is damaged beyond repair, and that belief makes him clamp down harder, watch harder, avoid more. He finally sought help after realizing that he no longer recognized his own life as meaningful and was spending nights listening for intruders while old scenes replayed in his head. What he wants, cautiously, is not to erase the event but to stop living as though it is still happening; what he fears is that if he stops guarding against it, he will disappear into it completely.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly state in a single paragraph that triggers directly lead Walter to negative appraisals or distorted beliefs.
The vignette does not clearly show, within one paragraph, that Walter’s negative appraisals directly cause the trauma memory to become more active or intrusive.
The vignette does not clearly state in a single paragraph that the trauma memory itself leads Walter to negative appraisals or beliefs about himself or his future.
The vignette does not clearly show, within one paragraph, that Walter’s sense of threat directly generates negative appraisals or distorted beliefs.
The vignette does not clearly state in a single paragraph that Walter’s maladaptive strategies directly increase, create, or maintain triggers/reminders.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state in a single paragraph that triggers directly lead Walter to negative appraisals or distorted beliefs.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not clearly show, within one paragraph, that Walter’s negative appraisals directly cause the trauma memory to become more active or intrusive.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state in a single paragraph that the trauma memory itself leads Walter to negative appraisals or beliefs about himself or his future.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly show, within one paragraph, that Walter’s sense of threat directly generates negative appraisals or distorted beliefs.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state in a single paragraph that Walter’s maladaptive strategies directly increase, create, or maintain triggers/reminders. 
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."

A routine assignment can feel loaded because anything might change without warning, and his attention catches on photographs and sensory details before he is aware he is searching for them. When he is this keyed up, the old film starts running again. A creak in his apartment or the sight of an object that could be used as a weapon is enough to pull him back into the event, and afterward he takes it as further proof that something in him has been permanently altered. Each time the memory takes over so completely, he comes away convinced not just that the assignment was terrible, but that he himself has been changed into someone damaged and unlikely ever to feel normal again.

What frightens Walter most is not only the memory itself but what he has come to believe it means. He says that if he lets himself think about the disaster directly, he will not be able to handle it. Because he had come to believe he was too altered and too fragile to bear the memory, the way he managed his days began to feel like simple necessity: he kept himself distracted, spent impulsively for brief relief, and arranged his body near walls and exits because trusting himself to cope without those measures no longer seemed realistic to him. That conviction makes the fragments easier to stir up, not easier to contain; the more certain he is that remembering will overwhelm him, the more readily the old images and sensations break through, as if his mind keeps returning to the scene to test the danger he has assigned to it. He has come to believe he will never feel normal emotions again, and that nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore. Those convictions shape what he does every day. And the more he relied on those measures to get through the day, the more they seemed to prove their own premise to him: if he still needed to scan, position himself, and buy relief in quick bursts, then he must indeed be damaged, unable to cope, and unlikely to get his life back. He avoids letting his mind settle, buys things impulsively online and in stores for a brief sense of comfort or distraction, and arranges himself physically against walls and exits as if vigilance were the only thing holding him together. Over months, those habits have made reminders harder to escape: every restaurant without the right seat, every office chair with its back exposed, every image archive he tries to hurry past has become newly charged because his daily routines keep marking these situations as places where something is wrong. Yet the relief is short-lived. The spending leaves him ashamed and emptier; the constant positioning and scanning tell him the threat must be real; the effort not to think about the event only seems to make the memory more intrusive and unreal at the same time. He says it is like trying not to touch a bruise and ending up pressing on it all day.

The loop has tightened over the last year. Because he freezes when startled and spends so much energy monitoring his surroundings, he is less able to stay present during interviews and has pulled back from some assignments that once gave his life structure. At home he sits in restaurants only if he can face the door, and if he cannot, he leaves. In the office he dreads the image desk, yet when a photo catches him off guard the memory floods back so vividly that the rest of the day is organized around managing it. Each recurrence deepens his conviction that he is damaged beyond repair, and that belief makes him clamp down harder, watch harder, avoid more. He finally sought help after realizing that he no longer recognized his own life as meaningful and was spending nights listening for intruders while old scenes replayed in his head. What he wants, cautiously, is not to erase the event but to stop living as though it is still happening; what he fears is that if he stops guarding against it, he will disappear into it completely.
